title: TCS commits $7.4B to a one-gigawatt AI campus in Hyderabad
content:
Tata Consultancy Services said its HyperVault unit and partners have committed 700 billion rupees, about $7.4B, to an AI data centre campus of up to one gigawatt in Hyderabad, using green energy and water-neutral design principles. EU rules require any data centre above 500kW to report total and drinking water consumption to a European database every year.
Tata Consultancy Services said its HyperVault unit and partners have committed 700 billion rupees, about $7.4B, to an AI data centre campus in southern India. Bloomberg News reported the exchange filing on Saturday.
The site sits on 264 acres in Hyderabad, in Telangana, and will have a capacity of up to one gigawatt. The land is already secured, and TCS expects the campus to rank among the largest AI infrastructure sites in India.
“The campus will support frontier AI companies and hyperscalers with high-density, liquid-cooled compute infrastructure on a global scale,” the company said.
TCS also says the project will use green energy and water-neutral design principles. Neither term is defined in the filing.
The money follows a pattern. TPG put $1B into the company’s data centre business last November, part of a wider flow of foreign capital into Indian AI infrastructure through local firms.
Two of those words carry obligations in Europe that they do not carry in India, and the gap is not rhetorical.
Any data centre in the EU with at least 500kW of installed IT power must report annually to a European database, under a delegated regulation adopted in 2024.
The indicators include total water consumption and drinking water consumption, from which water usage effectiveness is calculated. Energy demand, waste heat recovery and the renewable share are in there too.
The annual deadline is 15 May. The regulation itself sets out no penalty for not filing, so the discipline is disclosure rather than enforcement.
So water-neutral design is a phrase in Hyderabad and a filed number in Frankfurt. Neither guarantees the water, but only one leaves evidence.
The scale runs the other way. Europe has opened bidding for up to seven AI gigafactories worth roughly EUR 30B, of which about EUR 10B would be public money and only around EUR 1B of Brussels’ share is committed.
Construction there is targeted for early 2027. TCS is putting $7.4B into one campus now, most of it private money rather than public.
Europe built the measuring regime first and the gigawatts second. Its own gigafactory plan has already stumbled on delays, and this filing is what the other order looks like.

report.summary: TCS commits $7.4B to a one-gigawatt AI data center campus in Hyderabad, underscoring India's private AI infrastructure boom and Europe's contrasting disclosure-first approach.
report.background: India is becoming a major destination for AI infrastructure investment, driven by data localisation, rapid cloud adoption, and foreign capital flowing through domestic IT firms. Tata Consultancy Services, one of the country’s largest software exporters, is now entering the physical layer through its HyperVault unit. The $7.4B Hyderabad campus, on 264 acres, aims to meet demand from frontier AI companies and hyperscalers for dense, liquid-cooled compute. The project comes after TPG put $1B into TCS’s data-centre arm last November, part of a broader pattern of international investors backing Indian AI buildout. But the announcement also highlights regulatory asymmetry. In Europe, any data centre above 500kW must report water and energy usage annually under a 2024 delegated regulation; in India, terms such as 'green energy' and 'water-neutral' remain undefined and unverified claims. Europe has focused on measurement first, while India is scaling first. That difference shapes how these projects are monitored and disclosed.
key_points: TCS and partners are investing 700 billion rupees ($7.4B) to build an AI data-centre campus of up to one gigawatt on 264 acres in Hyderabad. TCS says it will be among India's largest AI infrastructure sites, offering high-density, liquid-cooled compute for hyperscalers and frontier AI companies.

The filing describes the facility as using green energy and water-neutral design, but neither term is defined. This matters because the same phrases carry legal meaning in the EU, where data centres over 500kW must report annual water usage, energy demand and renewable share to a European database by May 15.

Investment flows show growing foreign interest: TPG injected $1B into TCS’s data-centre business in November, and this new campus is mostly private money. The commitment puts TCS ahead of Europe's planned AI gigafactories, which have only about EUR1B of Brussels' share committed so far and target construction in 2027.

Europe's approach is disclosure-first: a delegated regulation sets no penalty for failing to file, making transparency the discipline. India's order is scale-first, so environmental claims in Hyderabad may not leave the kind of measured, auditable evidence that Frankfurt would require.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this signals India's emergence as a serious alternative to US and EU data-centre hubs, with gigawatt-scale private capital and a permissive regulatory environment. Developers and enterprises could gain access to large, liquid-cooled compute infrastructure that was previously concentrated in the US, potentially lowering costs and latency for AI workloads in South Asia. However, regular users and communities may bear environmental costs if 'green' and 'water-neutral' claims are not validated. The contrast with Europe is instructive: measurement before scale creates evidence, while scale before measurement creates risk. For TCS and India, the opportunity is huge, but the lack of binding reporting obligations leaves the burden on companies to prove sustainability. Watch whether investors and clients begin demanding consistent, comparable metrics.
report.tools: For those following data-centre sustainability, watch the EU's official Data Centre Reporting database and the 2024 delegated regulation register. Open-source projects worth exploring include the Open Compute Project's liquid-cooling designs, the Green Software Foundation's Carbon Intensity (SCI) methodology, and Electricity Maps for real-time clean-energy tracking. For water accounting, the Alliance for Water Stewardship and WULCA's water-scarcity footprint tool are helpful references.
